articles.title: A doctor, four clubs, and a beginning
articles.intro: Dr W. M. Brown brought an enthusiasm for golf to Tauranga. Within a year of his arrival, a club was taking shape.
paragraphs: Brown arrived from Dunedin in 1903. The book identifies a Bay of Plenty Times report of 20 April 1904 as the earliest written evidence of a golf club being formed in Tauranga. That distinction matters: 1903 begins this collection, while 1904 is the foundation year supported by the book.

By May 1905, the newspaper was reporting Brown’s re-election as captain and J. Bull’s re-election as secretary. The re-elections are another indication that this was already an established organisation.

The history recalls Brown arriving in a two-wheel gig driven by Arthur Faulkner. His bag held just four hickory-shafted clubs: a driver/brassie, cleek, lofter and putter. Ossie Daines carried them for sixpence. These details come from recollections assembled in the book, rather than surviving club minutes.
In June 1906, members of the golf and other local clubs joined a farewell dinner for Brown at the Masonic Hotel. His stay was short, but the game he helped establish endured.

articles.title: Golf between the Domain and the sea
articles.intro: Rugby players, tidal water and grazing animals were part of the challenge on Tauranga’s first course.
paragraphs: The early course began at Wharepai Domain and extended below The Elms towards Sulphur Point. The book describes a route through shared recreation grounds and low-lying coastal land, with a tin shed serving as a clubhouse.
One hole crossed the rugby ground. Another led to a green surrounded by water at high tide, reached by stepping-stones. The hazards were inseparable from the landscape and its other uses.

A surviving course card reproduced in the book records nine holes totalling 1,860 yards, with a bogey rating of 38. The longest hole, The Camp, measured 420 yards. Bogey was then used in the sense now associated with par.

The card is useful evidence, but its exact date is unresolved. Mowat notes that one hole is named Anzac, which raises a question about how that name fits the card’s presumed early date. It should not be treated as an independently dated 1904 document.

Conditions also changed over time: the 1908 meeting report describes a competition requiring two rounds of an eight-hole course. The book speculates about the missing hole; this preview leaves the reason open.

articles.title: A new home at Gate Pa
articles.intro: The move to the Racecourse Reserve gave the club room to grow, but making a course took the work of its members.
paragraphs: The foreword places the first approaches to the Racecourse Reserve trustees in 1913. In 1914, the club took up a lease at the reserve and moved away from the increasingly crowded Domain grounds.

The land was exposed and initially unpromising. Members cleared gorse, protected greens with fences, built stiles and prepared the ground. Auckland professional Fred Rutter was engaged to lay out eighteen holes, including holes inside the racecourse oval.

The first lease was for seven years. That offered a home for golf without the long-term security the club would later obtain. The course became known as Gate Pa, although the book points out that the reserve is in Greerton.

A transport notice reproduced on page 27, dated 20 June 1914, arranged Saturday cars from the corner of Wharf Street and The Strand. Players had to tell the secretary by Friday night if they wanted a seat.

The photograph reproduced with that notice shows The Avenue, the original first hole (identified in the 2014 book as the eleventh). The photograph itself is not dated; its appearance alongside a 1914 notice does not establish when it was taken.

articles.title: Making a club from a tin shed
articles.date: Early Gate Pa years · dates not specified
articles.intro: Working bees, shared lunches and the seasonal rhythm of golf sustained the early club.
paragraphs: The book describes a corrugated iron shed shared with the racing club as the first clubhouse at the reserve. A long table and forms occupied most of the room; primus stoves and kettles supplied tea.
Members brought paper-wrapped lunches, and many cycled to the course with clubs on their backs. A cookhouse and stove came later, although the passage does not give a precise year for the change.

Golf was largely a winter activity. In summer, the fairways produced hay; greens were prepared for a new season in March. Grazing animals and an occasional horse-drawn mower helped maintain the playing areas.
The women’s committee catered for visiting players under difficult conditions. Mowat records meals prepared at home and brought to the club, alongside the work of cleaning and preparing the shed.

These passages describe the early Gate Pa years broadly. They are included as context, rather than assigned to a particular year between 1914 and 1923. The accompanying golfing-party photograph is also undated and is not identified as a view of this shed.

articles.title: Names on the early honours boards
articles.intro: The championship lists preserve a dated thread through years for which other records are incomplete.
paragraphs: A. Matheson won the men’s senior championship in 1911 and 1912, and again in 1921. The introduction explains how the honours boards beginning in 1911 helped that year become accepted for a time as the club’s foundation date. The later research presented in the book instead supports 1904.

The men’s list records H. Phillips in 1913, no championship played in 1914, J. Fowles in 1915 and 1916, R. Renshaw in 1917, H. J. Rowe in 1918, and R. H. Roache in 1919. It gives Renshaw again in 1920, 1922 and 1923. The list does not explain why the 1914 championship was not played.

The women’s senior championship list begins in 1919 with Mrs G. Henderson. Miss R. Daines won in 1920, 1921 and 1922; Miss N. Wallis is listed for 1923. A separate biographical passage identifies the three-time winner as Rennie Daines.
The women’s list starting in 1919 should not be read as evidence that women only began playing then: the book names women members and mixed competition much earlier.
These names close the preview in 1923. The collection can grow into later decades using the same source references and article structure.

articles.title: A club finding its stride
articles.intro: Photographs and championship records show a growing club before the major changes of the 1930s.
paragraphs: The championship lists offer one way into the interwar years. The men’s senior title went to G. Pott in 1924 and 1926, R. P. Baigent in 1925 and A. Matheson in 1927. The women’s list records Mrs D. V. Hanna in 1924 and 1926, Mrs R. Burke in 1925 and Miss C. Humphreys in 1927.

The book’s profile of Elsie Hanna says she arrived in Tauranga in 1922 and served on the Ladies’ committee from 1926 to 1939. Such service is another part of the record alongside the championship results.

A photograph of closing day in 1931 gathers members outside the jockey’s room, which served as the early clubhouse. Other photographs identify Connie Humphreys in 1927 and a group at lunch in 1932. They give faces and everyday settings to an otherwise sparse written record.

The course still included holes within the racecourse oval. An old scorecard reproduced on page 29 records that earlier layout; the book describes a substantial redesign in 1934. These images and records provide a bridge from the first Gate Pa years to the next phase of development.

articles.title: Beyond the racecourse oval
articles.intro: A redesign helped transform the early Gate Pa layout into a more settled golf course.
paragraphs: The original Gate Pa course extended into the racecourse oval. In its account of 1934, the book describes the club commissioning Auckland professional Alex Murray to advise on a new layout.

The review removed the five holes using the oval and changed other parts of the route. Members had also hoped to avoid the demanding climbs associated with The Drop and The Hummocks. Retained holes were renumbered around the new sequence.

The account links this change with a growing determination to move beyond makeshift playing conditions. References to present-day hole numbers in the book describe the course as it stood in 2014; they should not be assumed to describe every later alteration.

One date needs care: page 37 associates the 1934 changes with a new 33-year lease, while page 23 places the board’s authority to grant that lease term in 1944. This preview retains the stated redesign date but does not use the disputed lease detail to explain it. The original lease and course records would help settle that point.

articles.title: Professional help, a new chapter
articles.intro: James Mowat and experienced greenkeeper W. H. Coles arrived as the club sought better golf and better playing conditions.
paragraphs: The history reproduces a Bay of Plenty Times report dated 30 March 1936 announcing two appointments: W. H. Coles as greenkeeper and James Mowat as the club’s professional.

Coles had worked at Napier Golf Club. Mowat came from Poverty Bay with experience in Scotland and the United States. The report presented their skills as an opportunity to improve both the course and the standard of play.

Tuition mattered for beginners and established golfers alike. The report emphasised the value of learning sound habits early and having someone able to identify faults in a more experienced player’s swing.

James was Dave Mowat’s father. The book’s introduction acknowledges that family connection, and its later account recalls James supporting junior golfers’ right to enter club championships during the 1950s. His contribution ran beyond the professional appointment itself.

articles.title: A clubhouse of their own
articles.intro: The shared tin shed gave way to a dedicated clubhouse, a milestone recorded in photographs.
paragraphs: The first Gate Pa clubhouse was a corrugated iron building shared with racing. The history describes crowded seating, shared lunches and the small comforts members gradually added to it.
In 1938 a dedicated clubhouse was built on the area the 2014 book identifies as the car park. Photographs record its opening and show Miss Eva Goodyear beside the trophies.

Two further views show the wooden building and the open ground around it. The building date is known, but those views are not individually dated. They show the clubhouse built in 1938 without establishing that each photograph was taken that year.

After the war the building could no longer comfortably serve the enlarged membership. When a new clubhouse opened in 1954, the old wooden structure was sold and moved to Pyes Pa, where the book says it became a home again.

articles.title: Nine holes and a different purpose
articles.intro: During the Second World War, part of the course was put to food production while a smaller course remained in play.
paragraphs: The book describes the course being reduced to nine holes during the war. The eighth, ninth and tenth fairways were ploughed and planted with potatoes, while other areas were left to grow hay.
Greenkeeper Mr Reeves maintained the remaining nine holes with limited equipment. The racecourse and its buildings also served as headquarters for the National Reserve, with members training there.

The Ladies’ minutes summarised in the history record fundraising for the Patriotic Shop in 1940. These contributions place the club within the wider demands of wartime, beyond the reduced playing programme.

The men’s senior championship appendix records no competition from 1941 to 1945. Accounts of the women’s wartime championships vary within the book: the appendix lists Anne Mark in 1941, while her profile describes that year as a gap. That discrepancy remains open for checking rather than being silently resolved.

articles.title: A course restored, a membership growing
articles.intro: Returning players and increasing membership brought new energy—and new demands on the club.
paragraphs: After the war, members worked to restore the full eighteen-hole course. The history associates that effort with returning servicemen and women eager to resume peacetime pursuits.
By 1951 the book records 416 members, an unprecedented total for the club. The wooden clubhouse that had opened in 1938 was becoming too small for the number of people using it.
The next phase included plans for a new building and continued improvement in course care. Grant Silvester took over as head greenkeeper in 1951, beginning a long association with the course.

This was more than a recovery of the prewar routine. It set up the clubhouse project, the Veterans’ Society and the expanded tournament programme that would make the 1950s such an active decade. The accompanying image shows the clubhouse built in 1954, after this period of growth.
Access improved as well: the book records sealing the first section of the entrance road in 1958, with the remaining section completed in 1960. The latter improvement falls just beyond this chapter.

articles.title: Building for a bigger club
articles.intro: Members helped finance a new clubhouse as postwar growth outstripped the old building.
paragraphs: The history records the sale of four hundred £10 debentures to help finance a new brick clubhouse. Alan Davidson, Dave Cambie and Lionel Smith formed the building committee.
The new building opened in 1954, on the site used by the later clubhouse. Photographs on page 55 show two views of the building, with the putting area and open course beside it.

The old wooden clubhouse was sold and relocated to Pyes Pa. The choice of the new building’s position had prompted debate, a reminder that even a widely welcomed improvement could raise different views among members.

The financial figures need verification: page 53 describes a construction ceiling of £5,700 and completion below budget; the later committee summary gives a cost of £5,750. Those passages may use different cost bases, but the book does not settle that question. The debenture record and opening year are presented separately from the unresolved final cost.

articles.title: The work behind the Wednesday game
articles.intro: Committee records show women shaping competition, fundraising and opportunities to play.
paragraphs: The book’s extracts from the Ladies’ minutes record a 1937 discussion about separating the men’s and ladies’ sections. The proposal was not adopted at that time. Later entries show the women organising competitions and undertaking essential work around the clubhouse.

In 1946 businesswomen asked to play their competitions on Saturday afternoons. The source records the request without giving the response. It is a small but telling example of how access to playing time mattered.

The 1952 minutes describe a Ways and Means Committee for the building programme. In 1953, the committee resolved that competition results and club news should be published in the Bay of Plenty Times; in 1954, a vote established Wednesday as club day.

Dr Jean Reading introduced a competition for school-age girls in 1955. The following year the minutes recorded insufficient interest to continue it. This short-lived initiative belongs in the junior story as well as the women’s record: encouragement did not always produce an enduring programme on its first attempt.

articles.title: Anne Mark: playing and making things happen
articles.intro: A player and administrator whose contribution reached well beyond her own competitions.
paragraphs: Anne Mark joined the club in 1935. Her recollections include helping Elsie Hanna prepare catering by gathering kindling and cutting firewood for the racing club’s range.
She first served as handicap manager in 1938 and held several positions on the Ladies’ committee. Her account in the book describes a practical involvement in the daily work that kept the club going.

Anne also assisted the Veterans’ Society with its first five-day tournament in 1953, working alongside Rennie Gordon, later Wallis. The Veterans’ history credits the two women with the clerical organisation behind those early tournaments.

In her account, Anne places the formation of the Bay of Plenty Ladies’ Golf Association in 1954 and records serving as its president for three years. She joined the national Ladies’ Golf Union council in 1955. Those roles connect the local club’s story to the wider administration of women’s golf.

articles.title: Una Wickham and the wider golfing world
articles.intro: A Tauranga player whose achievements connected the club to provincial and national golf.
paragraphs: Una Wickham joined Tauranga Golf Club in 1954 and represented Bay of Plenty in the Russell Grace interprovincial tournament that year. The team won, with further wins recorded in 1955 and 1959.

The book describes Una’s earlier international experience and her interest in more demanding playing conditions for leading women. It also records resistance to her choice of slacks in cold weather, illustrating the conventions women competitors faced.
At club level she began a run of seven consecutive senior championship wins in 1954. The appendix lists her as champion in every year from 1954 through 1959, the end of this chapter’s coverage.

In 1959 she won the New Zealand amateur championship, an achievement identified both in her profile and beside her portrait. Her later record extends well beyond the 1950s and will be developed in a future chapter. The portrait itself is undated; the caption lists titles rather than fixing when the photograph was taken.

articles.title: The beginnings of the Veterans’ Society
articles.intro: Friendly rounds grew into an organised society and an ambitious annual tournament.
paragraphs: The Veterans’ history traces the group’s origins to informal games after the Second World War. In 1952 it became an organised association, with John McKenzie as president and Dick Phelan as secretary.

In November 1953, a group of just 23 members staged a five-day tournament. Anne Mark and Rennie Gordon assisted with the organisation, and the event established a pattern that would continue for many years.

The group adopted the name Veterans’ Society in the mid-1950s to distinguish itself from the national association. In 1955 its summer programme included the Angus Plate, donated by Gavin Wallace. Veterans’ day changed to Thursday in 1957.

Tauranga hosted the national veterans’ championship in 1959. E. S. Toogood of Poverty Bay won, with Tauranga’s Frank Macklow runner-up. These events give the Senior Men collection an early foundation; later service projects and present-day activities can be added as separate records.

Much of this section of the book reproduces a 1977 history compiled by Bill Sanders and Ken McIntyre. The main narrative dates the first five-day tournament to 1953; a later passage mentions a 1951 tournament. This preview follows the explicit 1953 account and leaves the inconsistent reference noted for review.

articles.title: Inviting New Zealand to Tauranga
articles.intro: A national invitation tournament helped show the course to players and spectators beyond the district.
paragraphs: The 1952–53 committee wanted to attract visiting golfers and new members. Working with the New Zealand PGA, it planned a 54-hole invitation tournament for June 1953.

The first field included eighteen professionals and forty-two invited amateurs. Frank Buckler led the professionals with 216, four ahead of Alex Murray. Tori Jones of Taumarunui headed the amateur field by one stroke.

The event returned through the decade. The book records a round of 64 by Alex Murray in 1954, another win for Buckler in 1955, and a commanding performance by amateur Stuart Jones in 1956. Local professional Jimmy Paterson won the professional division that year.

The ambition was both to promote the course and to let younger players see leading golfers in action. The illustrated Labour Weekend group, dated approximately 1950, belongs to the wider tournament culture at the club; it is not a photograph of the 1953 invitation event.

articles.title: Opening the way for younger players
articles.intro: The book recalls a debate over schoolboys’ championship eligibility and an early competition for schoolgirls.
paragraphs: Dave Mowat records that Michael Cambie and Robert Mowat qualified for club championships during the 1950s but encountered objections because they were schoolboys paying junior subscriptions.

James Mowat and others supported their right to compete. According to the account, those arguments prevailed and the boys were allowed to participate. The recollection does not give an exact year, so this story remains dated to the decade.

The Ladies’ minutes record a different attempt to encourage younger players: Dr Jean Reading’s 1955 competition for school-age girls. It did not continue the following year because there was insufficient interest.

The photograph of Labour Weekend contenders around 1950 includes a barefoot caddie identified in the book as Brian Ducker. It shows another way younger people encountered the game. The boy in that image is not identified as either of the championship players discussed here.

articles.title: A shorter round, a wider welcome
articles.intro: Tauranga played a pioneering role in nine-hole golf, with Phyll Sandlant helping turn an invitation to try the game into a substantial club group.
paragraphs: The book describes a 1977 move to provide nine-hole handicaps for women who found a full round difficult. It presents that local provision as a forerunner of the later organised movement.

In Phyll Sandlant’s account reproduced by Mowat, an advertisement in February 1998 invited women to try nine-hole golf at Tauranga. Ninety-six women registered. Professional Rick Barker provided coaching, with volunteers accompanying beginners and introducing the game’s etiquette and competition formats.

The inaugural BOPTV Honda Nine Hole Tournament followed at Tauranga in 1999. The book credits Phyll and the volunteers who supported her, as well as Alison Holdem and Lynn Goodhew who carried the work forward. Phyll became a life member in 2006.

A separate 2014 centenary report in SunLive identifies Patsy Hankins as instrumental in the national initiative and says she approached Phyll in 1998 to help implement it. That report calls Tauranga the first New Zealand club; Phyll’s account in the book specifically describes the first group in Bay of Plenty. Both sources show Tauranga’s pioneering contribution, while describing the scope differently.

This story is included through the Ladies 9 Hole collection even though its dates fall beyond the historical chapters currently developed. Present-day membership, programmes and achievements can be recorded here as new, dated contributions rather than assumed from the 2014 account.
